report.releaseDate: 15 Oct 2026 (LGCB/LSP monthly revenue reports for September 2026; sportsbook workbooks dated 13 Oct 2026)
report.currency: USD (tables in US$ millions unless stated; market reports natively in USD)
report.verdict: September 2026 was Louisiana's best handle month of the year at $405.1m (+0.9% YoY), but a soft 10.7% hold cut net proceeds 8.0% to $43.4m and state tax 9.4% to $8.9m — the sportsbook market is now mature, 95% mobile, parlay-dependent (63% of mobile win) and taxed at 21.5%. The land-based base is the growth story for once ($195.5m casino GGR, +11.8% on landside relocations and Caesars New Orleans), while the rule-set is hardening: sweepstakes are banned with racketeering exposure from 1 Aug 2026, and a prop/micro-bet ban was shelved only because it would cost the state >$20m a year.
summary: **Best handle month of 2026, weakest hold since February:** total sports wagers of $405.1m (+0.9% YoY, +48.9% MoM as football returned) produced net proceeds (GGR after promo deductions) of $43.4m, down 8.0% YoY, because hold fell to 10.72% from 11.76%. Gross win before the $1.3m promo deduction was $44.7m (-7.5%), matching the ~$45m / -7% figure carried by trade press.

**Mobile is the market:** mobile handle $384.5m (+4.6% YoY) is 94.9% of stakes and $39.6m (91%) of net proceeds; retail handle collapsed 39.0% to $20.6m, although an 18.9% retail hold lifted retail win 30.6% to $3.9m. Mobile hold of 10.29% vs 12.03% a year ago explains the entire NP decline.

**Tax take tracked hold, not rate:** $8.88m paid in September (-9.4% YoY) — $8.50m mobile at exactly 21.5% of net proceeds and $0.38m retail at ~10% (9.7% effective after loss carry-forwards). September 2025 already carried the 21.5% rate, so there is no rate tailwind left in the YoY comparison.

**Fiscal Q1 FY27 (Jul–Sep 2026):** handle $956.7m (+6.4%), net proceeds $110.9m (-1.1%), tax $23.0m (+8.3%). The tax line grew only because July 2025 was the last month taxed at 15%; hold compressed to 11.6% from 12.5%.

**Calendar 2026 to date:** 9M handle $2,998m (+1.8% vs 9M-25 $2,945m), net proceeds $357.1m (+3.4%), tax $74.6m, promo deductions $31.4m (1.0% of handle). CY2025 closed at $4,245m handle / $521.5m NP / $92.7m tax — growth has decelerated to low single digits on stakes.

**FY26 (Jul-25–Jun-26) was the step-change year:** handle $4,241m (+5.7%), net proceeds $534.5m (+14.1%), tax $109.6m (+55.7%) as the mobile rate rose from 15% to 21.5% (Act 298 of 2025, effective 1 Aug 2025). Mobile: $3,996m / $505.1m / $106.6m; retail: $244.9m (-13.0%) / $29.4m / $2.9m. FY25 had grown +20.3% on handle, so the market has roughly halved its growth rate in a year.

**Product mix is parlay-led:** parlays generated $24.9m, 63% of September mobile net proceeds; football $5.2m, 'other' (props/tennis/golf/etc.) $6.4m, baseball $2.1m, basketball $0.8m, soccer $0.4m. FY26 parlays were $357.7m of $505.1m mobile NP (71%). This is the economic engine and the political target (see SB 354).

**Market structure (FY25, regulator-reported):** statewide gaming revenue ~$3,625m — riverboats $1,811.0m (50%), video poker net device revenue $757.7m (21%), mobile sports $442.6m (12%), racino slots $317.5m (9%), Caesars New Orleans land-based $270.1m (7%), retail sports $25.1m (1%), DFS net $1.5m. 'Online penetration' is therefore ~12% of gaming revenue and is sports-only: there is no iGaming and no iLottery.

**Land-based is growing double digits in Sep-26:** $195.5m (+11.8%), with the 16 riverboat/land-based casinos at $172.3m (+14%). Lake Charles $69.7m (+9.4%), New Orleans $50.4m (+13.8%; Caesars New Orleans $25.4m, +30.4%), Shreveport/Bossier $47.6m (+15.9%; Live! +31.3%), Baton Rouge $22.3m (+10.7%; Bally's Baton Rouge +607% after its landside move). Racetracks lag: Delta Downs $12.2m (-2.2%), Evangeline Downs $5.5m (-2.8%). Jefferies puts Q3 statewide GGR at +3.5% against an +8.3% comp.

**Licensing is capped and casino-anchored:** the Sports Wagering Act allows up to 20 sports wagering licences, reserved for the 15 riverboat, 4 racino and 1 land-based casino licensees; mobile is offered through platform providers (permit: $100,000 non-refundable application + $250,000 permit fee per five-year term) and service providers ($10,000 + $12,500). The LGCB platform list names 10 sportsbooks — FanDuel, DraftKings, Caesars, BetMGM, bet365, Fanatics, BetRivers, Bally Bet, ESPN Bet and TwinSpires — but several are understood to be inactive [current status unverified]; the regulator publishes no operator-level data, so shares are n/a.

**Tax regime (base = net proceeds, i.e. GGR less promo wagers, with operator losses carried forward):** mobile 21.5%, retail 10%; DFS 8% of net revenue; riverboats pay a 21.5% state fee on net gaming proceeds ($389m on $1,811m in FY25) plus local admission fees; racino slots paid $48m (15% effective state fee) and Caesars New Orleans $65.0m under its operating contract; video poker franchise fees are 22.5% for racetrack/OTB (Type 4) locations and higher for other location types [other rates unverified], $229.6m in FY25 (30% blended).

**Tax allocation politics:** Act 298 earmarks 25% of mobile sports tax to the SPORT Fund for public-university athletics (~$1.7–2m per Division I programme) and 3% to the Postsecondary Inclusive Education Fund, alongside the legacy split (25% early-childhood education, 10% local governments, 3% problem gambling). The original HB 639 draft proposed 32.5% — the legislature has shown both appetite and a ceiling.

**State take:** roughly $802m across all verticals in FY25 (22% blended on $3,625m), of which sports betting was only $70.4m; lifetime sports wagering since launch (retail Oct-21, mobile Jan-22) is $16.2bn handle, $1.85bn net proceeds and $312.6m tax.

**Enforcement has turned hard-edged:** HB 883 (dual-currency sweepstakes defined as illegal 'gambling by computer'; fines up to $100,000 per violation; liability extended to platform providers and payment processors; AG cease-and-desist and injunction powers) and HB 53 (gambling by computer, electronic sweepstakes devices and sports bribery added to the racketeering statute — up to 50 years and $1m) were signed in May 2026 and took effect 1 Aug 2026, after the Governor vetoed a 2025 sweepstakes ban and the LGCB issued 40+ cease-and-desist letters.

**Prop/micro-bet ban shelved purely on fiscal grounds:** SB 354 (ban on all proposition and in-play micro wagers from 1 Aug 2026) was withdrawn on 1 Apr 2026 after the fiscal note showed >$20m of annual General Fund loss (~$40m total tax in some reports); the sponsor has said she will return in 2027. With parlays and props carrying ~70% of mobile win, this is the single biggest product risk in the state.

**No iGaming, no iLottery, grey-zone prediction markets:** no online casino bill advanced in 2026; an iLottery authorisation was prefiled [outcome unverified]; federally-regulated event contracts (Kalshi et al.) remain outside the LGCB framework [enforcement status unverified]. The 'online' TAM is therefore capped at sportsbook NP of ~$500–535m a year.

**Payments and RG:** the regulator publishes no payments data; deposits run on standard US rails (ACH, cards, wallets, casino-cage cash) with no state credit-card ban identified [unverified]. Minimum age 21, parish-level geofencing (55 of 64 parishes opted in), a statewide LGCB self-exclusion list, 3% of sports tax to problem gambling, and an LGCB prohibition on college player props (since 2024) [not re-verified].

**Read-through for B2Tech:** B2C market access requires a skin agreement with one of the 20 casino/racino licensees, a $350k permit outlay and competing for share in a FanDuel/DraftKings-dominated market growing 2–6% on handle and taxed at 21.5% of a promo-deductible base — expensive share-taking, not greenfield. The more realistic angle is B2B (platform/service-provider permits are cheap) and supplying land-based operators, who are the only growing, protected segment; keep any grey-market adjacency (sweeps, prediction markets) out of Louisiana entirely given racketeering exposure.

segments.name: Mobile sports betting (online)
segments.headline: $384.5m handle (+4.6%) but a 10.3% hold took net proceeds down 10.6% to $39.6m; parlays are 63% of win and the whole economic argument.
narrative: September is the first full football month and it duly reset the run-rate: mobile wagers of $384.5m were up 47.5% on August and 4.6% on September 2025, the strongest month of calendar 2026 and the third-highest ever behind October and November 2025 ($430.8m and $414.6m). The problem was margin. Mobile win before promo deductions was $40.9m, and after a $1.3m promotional-wager deduction net proceeds were $39.6m, a 10.3% hold against 12.0% a year earlier and 11.9% in August. Football net proceeds of $5.2m were 17% lower than September 2025's $6.2m on a larger handle, and the 'other' bucket (props, tennis, golf, combat) fell from $9.9m to $6.4m, which is consistent with favourites covering in the early NFL and SEC weeks rather than any change in pricing. Parlay win of $24.9m was effectively flat year on year ($25.4m) and carried 63% of mobile net proceeds; baseball ($2.1m) and basketball ($0.8m) were seasonal filler and soccer ($0.4m) remains immaterial.

The longer series shows a market that has moved from expansion to maturity. Mobile handle grew 37% in FY24, 23% in FY25 and 7% in FY26; the fiscal first quarter of FY27 is running +9.8% on handle but -0.6% on net proceeds, and calendar 9M-2026 handle is only +1.8% versus 9M-2025. Hold has become the swing variable: the trailing-twelve-month figure is 12.4% on $4.30bn of handle and $533m of net proceeds, with monthly readings ranging from 10.3% (September) to 15.6% (December 2025). An operator underwriting Louisiana should model 11.5–12.5% structural net hold with ±2pp monthly noise, not the 14–15% seen in the November–December 2025 run.

Promotional deductions deserve attention because the base is uncapped. Across FY26 operators deducted $34.9m of promo wagers (0.9% of handle), but $25.6m of that landed in January–April 2026 — $12.0m in January alone, ten times the normal $1.0–1.3m monthly run-rate — before dropping back to $1.1–1.3m from May. Whatever the cause (a large operator's acquisition push or a reclassification), it shows the deduction can materially move the taxable base, which makes it a likely legislative target when the state next looks for revenue; September's deduction was a modest $1.3m, 0.3% of handle.

Tax paid of $8.50m in September equals 21.5% of net proceeds to the cent, confirming the Act 298 rate has been fully in force since August 2025 (July 2025 was still taxed at 15.0%). Lifetime, mobile has produced $14.8bn of handle, $1.70bn of net proceeds and $297m of tax. The sportsbook roster is the one thing the regulator does not quantify: the LGCB platform list names ten brands (FanDuel, DraftKings, Caesars, BetMGM, bet365, Fanatics, BetRivers, Bally Bet, ESPN Bet, TwinSpires) but publishes no operator-level handle, and at least two of those listings are understood to be dormant [unverified]; third-party guides count seven live apps. For B2Tech, the practical consequence is that share cannot be tracked from public data, and entry is only possible as a second skin on a casino licensee whose first skin is almost certainly already a top-four brand.

Guidance for the segment is implicit rather than official: the state's FY27 budget was built on the 21.5% rate and roughly $105–110m of sports tax (our reading of the FY26 $109.6m outturn), which requires net proceeds of ~$500m. On 9M-2026 net proceeds of $357m and a Q4-2025 comparison of $176m, calendar 2026 should land at $500–525m of net proceeds and $4.25–4.35bn of handle (estimates), i.e. flat-to-low-single-digit growth with hold risk to the downside.

segments.name: Retail sports betting
segments.headline: Retail handle fell 39% to $20.6m — structural migration to mobile — though an 18.9% hold produced a one-off 31% rise in win.
narrative: Retail sportsbooks inside the riverboats, racinos and Caesars New Orleans wrote $20.6m in September, down 39.0% from $33.8m a year earlier and the lowest September since launch in October 2021. The decline is not a one-month event: retail handle fell 13.0% in FY26 to $244.9m and is down 36.3% in the first quarter of FY27 at $42.3m; the trajectory is for roughly $150–170m of annual retail handle by FY27, or around 4% of the state total versus 10% in FY23. Net proceeds nonetheless rose 30.6% to $3.9m because the book held 18.9% — a function of casino-floor parlay and football tickets (parlays $2.2m and football $1.8m made up more than the entire win, with baseball, basketball and 'other' negative) rather than anything repeatable. Tax paid was $0.38m, 9.7% of net proceeds against a 10% statutory rate, with the gap explained by the loss carry-forward provision.

The retail channel matters less for its economics than for market access: every one of the 20 sports wagering licences is held by a land-based casino, and the statute's design — retail first (October 2021), mobile three months later — ties the mobile skins to those properties. The retail books are therefore an amenity that anchors the licence rather than a profit centre. FY26 retail net proceeds of $29.4m across up to 20 venues equate to roughly $1.5m per licence, before staff, kiosk and platform costs, which is why several licensees operate their retail book through the same platform provider that holds their mobile skin.

For an operator weighing the state, the retail numbers reinforce two points. First, the structural shift is complete: 95.6% of FY27 Q1 handle is mobile and retail has become a 2–4% channel whose cash-handling and cage integration still carries full compliance cost. Second, the loss carry-forward and the state's willingness to leave retail at 10% while raising mobile to 21.5% signal that the legislature views the casinos — the retail licence holders — as the constituency to protect; any future product restriction (such as the shelved SB 354) would hit mobile parlays far harder than casino-floor betting.

segments.name: Land-based casinos, racinos & video poker
segments.headline: September casino GGR of $195.5m (+11.8%) is the fastest growth in the state, driven by landside relocations and Caesars New Orleans; racetracks lag and video poker is the quiet $750m+ vertical.
narrative: The LGCB's September casino report shows statewide gaming revenue of $195.5m, up 11.8% year on year, with the 15 riverboats and the single land-based casino at $172.3m (+14%) and the four racino slot floors making up the ~$23m balance. Lake Charles — the Houston feeder market — remains the largest district at $69.7m (+9.4%), led by L'Auberge du Lac ($26.7m, +10.6%) and Golden Nugget ($25.1m, +14.3%), with Delta Downs softer at $12.2m (-2.2%). New Orleans rose 13.8% to $50.4m on the back of Caesars New Orleans ($25.4m, +30.4%), still lapping the $435m rebuild completed in October 2024, while Treasure Chest ($11.9m, -3.4%) and Boomtown ($7.3m, +2.6%) were flat. Shreveport/Bossier grew 15.9% to $47.6m, with Margaritaville ($11.9m, +17.8%), Horseshoe ($11.1m, +17.2%) and Live! ($10.5m, +31.3%) all double-digit as the market absorbs its new landside capacity; Baton Rouge was up 10.7% to $22.3m almost entirely because Bally's Baton Rouge moved ashore ($4.9m, +607%), masking declines at L'Auberge Baton Rouge (-6.9%) and the Queen (-16.4%). Evangeline Downs ($5.5m, -2.8%) and the other racetracks were the laggards; Jefferies' read is Q3 statewide GGR of +3.5% against an +8.3% prior-year comp, with Caesars the only operator to sustain momentum through the quarter.

The annual picture from the LGCB's 30th report to the legislature (FY2024-25) frames the scale. Riverboat adjusted gross revenue was $1,811.0m (+$79.7m, +4.6%), generating over $389m of state fees at the 21.5% rate, with Bossier City, Kenner and Baton Rouge growing and a $270m landside facility opening in February 2025; the Kenner/Harvey/Amelia group was $298.3m (+$58.4m) and Baton Rouge $275.2m (+$12.5m). Caesars New Orleans generated $270.1m (+$29.6m, +12.3%) and paid $65.0m under its operating contract, employing ~2,430 people. Slot machines at the four racetracks (Delta Downs, Evangeline Downs, Fair Grounds, Louisiana Downs) produced $317.5m, essentially flat, with $48m of state fees. Video poker — 12,199 devices at 1,386 truck stops, bars, restaurants, hotels and OTBs at June 2025, rising to 12,482 devices at 1,376 locations by October 2025 — generated $757.7m of net device revenue (+1.1%) and $229.6m of franchise fees (30% blended; Type 4 racetrack/OTB locations pay 22.5%), making it the second-largest vertical in the state and larger than mobile sports betting by 70%. Tribal casinos (Coushatta, Paragon, Cypress Bayou, Jena Choctaw Pines) report nothing to the Board under IGRA and are excluded from every figure above.

Commercially, the land-based market is closed to new entrants — riverboat and racino licences are capped by statute and change hands only via M&A (Bally's, Boyd, Caesars, Penn, Churchill Downs, Cordish/Live!, Golden Nugget/Fertitta are the incumbents) — but it is the segment where capital is being rewarded: the 2018 landside law continues to pull revenue up as boats relocate ashore, and the riverboats employed ~9,700 people in Q3 2025. For a technology supplier the relevant openings are cashless and cage integration, retail sportsbook kiosks and platform supply to licensees whose mobile skins remain unfilled; for a B2C sportsbook the casinos are the gatekeepers of market access and will price a second skin accordingly.

Two cautions. The September +11.8% is flattered by easy comps (Bally's Baton Rouge was mid-transition a year ago, and hurricane/weather effects in 2025 are not disclosed in the sources read), and the Q3 figure of +3.5% is the better run-rate. And the state's dependence on this base — ~$730m of FY25 fees from riverboats, Caesars, racinos and video poker versus $70m from sports — explains why every 2025–26 policy move has protected land-based incumbents while tightening the screws on online verticals.

segments.name: Licensing, tax & enforcement
segments.headline: Casino-anchored licensing (20 licences, $350k platform permits), a 21.5% mobile tax on a promo-deductible base, and a 2026 session that criminalised sweepstakes while shelving a prop-bet ban for fiscal reasons.
narrative: Louisiana regulates all commercial gaming through the Louisiana Gaming Control Board (LGCB), a five-member board whose enforcement, audit and revenue-reporting functions are delegated to the Louisiana State Police Gaming Enforcement Division; the Board's own operating budget was just $1.0m in FY25, funded from riverboat, sports-wagering and pari-mutuel enforcement funds. The enabling statutes are the Riverboat Economic Development and Gaming Control Act, the Economic Development and Gaming Corporation Act (Caesars New Orleans), the Video Draw Poker Devices Control Law, the Pari-mutuel Live Racing Facility Economic Redevelopment and Gaming Control Act, the Fantasy Sports Contests Act and the Sports Wagering Act (2021). Sports wagering is legal only in the 55 parishes that voted yes in November 2020; the nine that declined are geofenced out, which slightly reduces addressable population relative to the state's 4.6m residents.

The sports wagering licence structure is the critical constraint. The Board may award up to 20 sports wagering licences and only riverboat licensees, slots-at-the-track licensees and the land-based casino operator were eligible in the initial phase; each licensee may run its own sportsbook or contract a platform provider for retail and mobile. A platform provider permit costs a $100,000 non-refundable application fee plus a $250,000 permit fee for a five-year term (payable again at each five-year anniversary); a service provider permit (geolocation, KYC, odds feeds, risk management) costs $10,000 plus $12,500 for five years. Those are low by US standards — Louisiana's entry cost is a fraction of New York's or Pennsylvania's — but the binding cost is the commercial deal with a casino licensee, and with the LGCB listing ten platforms against a maximum of 20 licences the practical supply of skins is already concentrated among the largest brands. Mobile sportsbooks must also submit house rules and new wager types to the Board's Sports Wagering Catalog (version 78 issued 2 Sep 2026), which approves leagues and bet types individually.

Tax is levied on 'net proceeds' — wagers less payouts less promotional wagers — with statutory loss carry-forward, which is why monthly tax paid can deviate from the headline rate. Mobile pays 21.5% (Act 298 of 2025, HB 639, signed June 2025, effective 1 Aug 2025; the first draft proposed 32.5%); retail pays 10%; DFS pays 8% of net revenue. Riverboats pay a 21.5% state fee on net gaming proceeds plus parish/municipal admission fees; racinos pay state fees that came to ~15% of slot AGR in FY25 after purse and local allocations; Caesars New Orleans pays under its renewed operating contract ($65.0m in FY25); video poker franchise fees are 22.5% for Type 4 (racetrack/OTB) locations and higher for truck stops and bars [non-Type-4 rates not verified in this brief]. Act 298 also re-plumbed the dedications: 25% of mobile sports tax now goes to the SPORT Fund for NCAA Division I athletic departments at public universities (eleven programmes including LSU, roughly $1.7–2m each) and 3% to the Postsecondary Inclusive Education Fund, on top of the legacy 25% to early-childhood education, 10% to local governments and 3% to problem gambling. That creates a durable political constituency for keeping — or raising — the sports tax.

The 2026 regular session (March–June) produced the toughest enforcement regime of any US state. HB 883 (Rep. Schlegel; House 98-0, Senate 35-0) rewrote the 'gambling by computer' statute to cover dual-currency online games that simulate gambling and award cash-convertible prizes, extended liability to platform providers and financial-transaction providers, raised the maximum fine from $20,000 to $100,000 per violation (five-year prison exposure retained) and gave the Attorney General cease-and-desist and injunctive powers. HB 53 (Rep. Fontenot; House 86-11, Senate 27-9) added gambling by computer, electronic sweepstakes devices and sports-participant bribery to the state racketeering statute — up to 50 years' hard labour, $1m fines and a five-year mandatory minimum where more than $10,000 is involved. Both were signed in May 2026 and took effect 1 Aug 2026, after Governor Landry had vetoed the 2025 sweepstakes ban (SB 181) on the grounds that the LGCB already had the authority — which it then used, issuing 40+ cease-and-desist letters; the Board's 30th annual report explicitly credits these actions with stopping 'multiple illegal operators'. By contrast SB 354 (Sen. Jackson-Andrews), which would have banned all proposition and in-play micro bets from 1 Aug 2026, was withdrawn on 1 Apr 2026 once the Legislative Fiscal Office showed a General Fund loss exceeding $20m a year (around $40m of total tax in some accounts); the sponsor has said she will return with a revised bill in 2027. An iLottery authorisation was also prefiled [outcome unverified], and no iGaming bill advanced. The direction of travel is unambiguous: protect the taxed, licensed base (casinos, video poker, the big sportsbooks), criminalise anything adjacent, and keep the tax conversation open.

segments.name: Payments, responsible gambling & advertising
segments.headline: A conventional US payments stack with no regulator data, a modest RG framework (3% of sports tax, statewide self-exclusion, 21+, parish geofencing) and advertising rules that lean on the Board's catalog and wager approvals rather than hard caps.
narrative: Louisiana publishes no payments statistics, and nothing in the September release or the annual report quantifies deposit methods, failed transactions or withdrawal times. In practice the licensed mobile books run the standard US stack — ACH/online banking, debit and credit cards, PayPal/Venmo-type wallets, Apple Pay, PayNearMe cash vouchers and cash at the partner casino cage — and the state has not legislated a credit-card deposit ban of the kind adopted in some north-eastern states [unverified]. The relevant 2026 change is indirect: HB 883 extends 'gambling by computer' liability to financial-transaction providers that process dual-currency sweepstakes payments, which will push acquirers and processors to tighten merchant-category screening for anything that looks like unlicensed gaming in Louisiana from 1 Aug 2026. For a B2B supplier this raises the compliance bar on any payments product sold into the state and effectively eliminates the grey-market processing opportunity.

Responsible-gambling architecture is statutory but thin by European standards. The minimum age is 21 for all commercial gaming; sports wagers can only be placed by persons physically located in one of the 55 opted-in parishes, enforced by geolocation at the platform level; the LGCB runs a statewide self-exclusion list that applies across riverboats, Caesars New Orleans, racinos, video poker and sportsbooks; and 3% of sports wagering tax is dedicated to problem-gambling programmes (via the Louisiana Department of Health's Office of Behavioral Health, which runs the 1-877-770-STOP helpline). On the FY26 sports tax of $109.6m that is roughly $3.3m a year. There are no statutory deposit limits, affordability checks or mandatory loss limits; operators must offer self-set limits and cooling-off tools under Board rules. The Board prohibited proposition wagers on individual college athletes in 2024 [widely reported; not re-verified in this brief], which matters in an LSU-dominated market, and the Sports Wagering Catalog continues to gate every new league and bet type.

Advertising is regulated through licence conditions rather than a bespoke code: no marketing to under-21s or on college campuses, no misleading 'risk-free' framing, and mandatory responsible-gaming messaging and helpline inclusion; there is no whistle-to-whistle restriction, no affiliate licensing regime of note, and no bonus cap. The promotional-wager deduction means bonusing is tax-efficient, which is visible in the January–April 2026 surge to $25.6m of deductions. The political mood, however, is shifting: the SB 354 debate was framed explicitly around harm from in-play micro-betting to college-age bettors, and the sponsor's commitment to return in 2027 — together with the racketeering tool now available to the AG — means that advertising and product restrictions are the most likely next front once the sweepstakes campaign is complete. An operator should assume tighter in-play and prop rules, and possibly a cap on promo deductions, within a two-year horizon.

highlights.text: Mobile handle is still growing in a mature market — +4.6% YoY in September, +9.8% in fiscal Q1 and 95% of all stakes — on a $4.3bn trailing-twelve-month base that yields ~$530m of net proceeds; the addressable online pool is real even if growth is now mid-single-digit.

Parlay-led economics: parlays delivered $24.9m (63%) of September mobile win and 71% of FY26 mobile net proceeds; with the prop/micro-bet ban (SB 354) withdrawn, the high-margin product set stays intact through at least the 2026-27 season.

Tax base relief is built into the statute: promotional wagers are deductible and operator losses carry forward, so the 21.5% headline rate applies to a net base — FY26 promo deductions of $34.9m were worth ~$7.5m of tax at the mobile rate.

Land-based momentum: casino GGR +11.8% in September (16 casinos +14%), with landside relocations (Bally's Baton Rouge +607%, Shreveport/Bossier +15.9%) and Caesars New Orleans (+30.4%) proving that capex is being rewarded in a protected, capped licence environment.

The sweepstakes ban (HB 883/HB 53, effective 1 Aug 2026) removes an untaxed online-casino substitute that had been competing with licensed sportsbooks for the same wallets; licensed operators are the direct beneficiaries of the AG's new enforcement toolkit.

Entry costs for suppliers are low: a platform provider permit is $350k per five years and a service provider permit $22.5k, so a B2B route (platform, risk, payments, kiosks, cashless) into the 20 casino licensees and ~12,500-device video poker estate is cheap to secure relative to the state's ~$3.6bn gaming revenue.

Enforcement credibility is high and public: the LGCB's 40+ cease-and-desist letters and the annual report's explicit claim of having stopped multiple illegal operators give licensed participants a cleaner competitive field than most US states.

lowlights.text: Tax risk is live, not theoretical: the mobile rate rose 43% (15%→21.5%) in August 2025, the opening bid was 32.5%, and 28% of the take is now earmarked to college athletics and inclusive education — constituencies that will lobby for more, not less; a promo-deduction cap is the obvious next lever.

Hold compression hit the P&L: September mobile hold of 10.3% (vs 12.0%) turned +4.6% handle growth into -10.6% net proceeds; monthly hold has ranged 10.3–15.6% over the past year, so quarterly earnings from Louisiana are results-driven and volatile.
Retail is in structural collapse — handle -39% in September, -36% in fiscal Q1, -13% in FY26 — leaving casino-floor books as a compliance cost that anchors the licence rather than a profit centre.

Market access is gated: 20 licences held exclusively by casinos/racinos, ten platforms already listed, no operator-level data published, nine parishes geofenced out, and no iGaming or iLottery — a new B2C entrant must buy a second skin from an incumbent and take share from FanDuel/DraftKings in a market growing ~2% on calendar handle.

Product restriction is a 2027 risk: SB 354's prop and micro-bet ban died only on a >$20m fiscal note, and the sponsor has committed to refile; with parlays and 'other' wagers carrying ~79% of mobile win, even a partial in-play restriction would cut net proceeds and tax materially.

Racketeering exposure for anything adjacent: HB 53 makes 'gambling by computer' a RICO predicate (up to 50 years, $1m) and HB 883 reaches platform and payment providers; prediction-market and sweepstakes adjacencies carry criminal, not just civil, risk in Louisiana from 1 Aug 2026.

Data gaps limit diligence: the regulator reports no operator shares, no actives/ARPU, no payments data, and tribal casino revenue is undisclosed; September video poker and lottery figures were not available for this brief, so the total-market picture rests on FY25 annual data.

forecast.intro: A market has no guidance, so the bridge tracks how the rule-set has moved from the FY25 baseline (15% mobile tax, sweepstakes in a grey zone, props unrestricted, no online casino) to the regime in force for FY27. The tax step-up came from the legislature's 2025 budget-gap search and the college-athletics lobby; the enforcement step-up came from the LGCB and the Attorney General rather than new operators; and the one measure that would have hit the parlay-led mobile model — SB 354 — was stopped by the Legislative Fiscal Office's arithmetic, not by principle. Net effect for the September data: the same handle generates ~43% more tax per dollar of net proceeds than two years ago, while the grey-market competitors that were absorbing wallet share are being criminalised out of the state.

forecast.view: Our independent view is that Louisiana is a **mature, mobile-only sportsbook market growing 2–5% on handle** with a land-based base growing faster for the next two to three quarters as landside relocations annualise. For calendar 2026 we model (estimates) handle of **$4.25–4.35bn**, net proceeds of **$500–525m** (assuming Q4 hold reverts to 12–13% against Q4-25's exceptional $176m) and sports tax of **~$105–110m**; for FY27 we expect handle +3–5%, net proceeds flat to +5% and mobile share above 95%, with retail handle falling a further 25–35%. Trailing hold should normalise to **~12%**, and parlay share will stay above 60% of mobile win unless product rules change. On rules, we see **no change to the 21.5% rate before the FY28 budget cycle**, but a **better-than-even chance of a promo-deduction cap or an in-play/prop restriction being filed in the 2027 regular session**; the fiscal note on SB 354 shows the state values the product at >$20m of General Fund a year, which is also the price at which it would trade it away. Enforcement will intensify rather than relax — the AG now has racketeering tools and payment-processor liability — and we expect the first HB 883/HB 53 actions, and probably a Louisiana move against sports event contracts, before mid-2027. **No iGaming before 2028 at the earliest**: the casino and video poker constituencies (~$730m of state fees) have no incentive to cannibalise themselves, and the legislature's 2025–26 record is one of protecting them. For B2Tech, the implication is that Louisiana is a **B2B and land-based supply opportunity, not a B2C entry market**: platform, risk, kiosk, cashless and compliance-payments products sold to the 20 licensees and the video poker route, with no exposure to any grey-market adjacency.
watch: Q4-2026 football hold and handle against the Q4-2025 comp ($1.30bn handle, $176m net proceeds, 13.5% hold) — determines whether calendar 2026 net proceeds beat 2025's $521.5m.

2027 regular session prefilings (from ~January 2027): a refiled prop/micro-bet ban, any promo-deduction cap, mobile tax tweaks and the fate of iLottery; the SPORT Fund's first distributions will shape the political appetite.
First enforcement actions under HB 883/HB 53 after 1 Aug 2026 — targets, payment-processor involvement and whether sports event contracts (Kalshi/Robinhood/Crypto.com) are swept in.
LGCB platform-list refresh and any new skin agreements (Bally Bet, Fanatics, bet365 expansion; ESPN Bet/TwinSpires status) — the only public signal of operator churn in a market with no share data.
Landside relocation pipeline and racino weakness: Bally's Baton Rouge and Shreveport/Bossier comps lap in 2027; Delta Downs/Evangeline Downs declines may prompt racino relief requests.
Video poker device count (12,482 at Oct-25) and net device revenue — the second-largest vertical and the clearest read on the land-based consumer.
Promotional deductions: a repeat of the Jan–Apr 2026 $25.6m spike would both depress tax and invite a legislative cap.

report.confidenceNote: Market reports natively in USD; no FX conversion required. Sports-wagering figures (handle, promo deductions, net proceeds, hold, tax, product mix, fiscal/calendar aggregates) are taken directly from the LGCB/LSP September 2026 mobile and retail sportsbook workbooks and cross-check to Gaming Intelligence ($405.1m, +1%) and CDC Gaming ($45m gross win, -7%; $405m handle) — HIGH confidence. September 2026 casino/racino figures are LGCB data as relayed by CDC Gaming and Gaming Intelligence; the regulator's own casino workbook was not re-opened — MEDIUM. FY25 market composition, licence fees and state fees are from the LGCB 30th/29th Annual Reports and Board transcripts — HIGH. Legislative items (Act 298/HB 639, HB 883, HB 53, SB 354) are corroborated across the legislative digest and at least two trade sources — HIGH. NOT verified in this brief: September 2026 video poker and lottery data; operator-level shares (not published by the regulator); the current active status of ESPN Bet and TwinSpires on the LGCB platform list; the iLottery bill outcome; prediction-market enforcement status; non-Type-4 video poker franchise-fee rates; the absence of a credit-card deposit ban; the 2024 college player-prop prohibition. All forecast figures are our estimates and are labelled as such.
